info.title: MonitorFlow public API
info.description:
The public API of MonitorFlow, for scripts and integrations: a ticketing tool reading alerts, a chat bot acknowledging them, a deployment script silencing a server while it works. It is the same API the web interface uses, under `/api/v1`, with the same rules about who may see and change what.

## API keys

An administrator makes a key under **Admin › API keys**: a global administrator for anything, a customer's administrator for that customer, a site's administrator for that site. The key is shown once, when it is made: `mfk_` followed by 43 characters. MonitorFlow keeps only a hash of it, so a lost key cannot be shown again; make another one.

What a key may do is chosen when it is made and never changes. To change it, make another key and turn the first one off.

- **Access**: "Read only" (viewer, the default), "Read and change" (operator), "Approve commands" (approver) or "Administer" (administrator).
- **Reach**: everything, one customer or one site. Outside its reach, servers, sites and incidents do not exist for the key: they answer 404, and lists leave them out.
- **Areas**, all by default: `servers` (servers and relays, their metrics and logs), `alerts` (incidents, silences, on-call, follow-up, sensors, thresholds and check settings, offline alerts, notification channels), `updates` (commands, campaigns, packages, package sources, mirrors, rollback, update settings), `remediation` (AI remediation and AI commands), `dashboards`, and `administration` (everything else). A route outside the key's areas answers 403 `api_key_scope`. Any key may list servers, relays, sites and customers within its reach, to turn names into IDs. Each operation below says which area it belongs to.
- **Expiry**: 30 days, 90 days, 1 year (the default) or never.

A key acts as the person who made it, narrowed to its reach and access, checked again on every request. It never does more than its maker could at that moment: a maker who loses a role loses it for the key too, a maker who is disabled finds the key refused, and a maker who is deleted takes the key with them. The keys list shows when each key was last used, to the minute. Anyone who could have made a key can turn it off; it stops at its next request.

What a key changes is written to the audit log as its maker's action, with the key's ID, so the log tells a person from their script. The secret never appears in the audit log or the server's logs.

## Authentication

Send the key in the `Authorization` header of every request:

```
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer mfk_…" https://monitorflow.example.com/api/v1/servers
```

Keys work only under `/api/v1`; the web interface's own paths refuse them. A request with a key needs no CSRF header. A missing, malformed, unknown or expired key, or one whose maker is disabled, answers 401 `unauthenticated`.

Signing in and out, first-run setup, password and acknowledge links, display links and screens, API keys themselves, a person's own on-call contact, and inviting users or issuing their password links are not part of the public API: they answer 404 under `/api/v1`. They are for people in a browser, or they hand out a credential that would outlive the key.

## Versions and changes

`/api/v1` is a contract. Within v1, MonitorFlow only adds: new fields in answers, new optional parameters, new routes, new values of `code`. Fields are never renamed or removed and their types never change. Your client must ignore fields it does not know. When a change would break v1, MonitorFlow keeps the old shape in v1 and makes a v2 only when that becomes unreasonable.

This document is served by every central server at `/api/v1/openapi.json`, without a key.

## Conventions

- Bodies are JSON objects with `snake_case` field names. Send `Content-Type: application/json`. Bodies are at most 64 KiB; a larger one answers 413. Most routes refuse a body with a field they do not know, with 400 `invalid`.
- IDs are UUIDs. Times are RFC 3339 in UTC, like `2026-11-14T09:30:00Z`. Durations are in seconds (`_s`) or milliseconds (`_ms`), as the field name says.
- An ID that is not a UUID answers 404, like an ID that does not exist.

## Pagination

Lists that can grow without bound take `limit` and `cursor` and answer `next_cursor`: servers, relays, incidents, a server's commands and packages, campaigns, tokens, remediation incidents and events. Pass `next_cursor` as `cursor` to get the next page, with the same filters; it is `null` on the last page. Cursors are opaque: do not build or change them. A server or incident added between two pages neither repeats nor shifts the others. There are no page numbers or totals.

Lists that stay small (sites, customers, silences, approvals, dashboards) answer in full.

## Filters

Filters are query parameters, exact values ANDed together, like `GET /api/v1/incidents?state=open&severity=critical&site_id=…`. A bad value is 400 `invalid`, and so is an unknown parameter on the lists that say so.

## Errors

Every error answers with a status and a JSON body:

```json
{"error": "limit must be between 1 and 500", "code": "invalid"}
```

`error` is a sentence in plain words, safe to show to a person; it may change between versions. `code` is stable: branch on it. Codes are only ever added.

| Code | Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `invalid_request` | 400 | The body could not be read as JSON (most routes answer `invalid` instead, with the parser's message) |
| `invalid` | 400 | A parameter or field is wrong; `error` says which and why |
| `unauthenticated` | 401 | No key, or one that is unknown, expired or turned off, or whose maker is disabled |
| `invalid_credentials` | 401 | Wrong username or password (signing in, not in v1) |
| `forbidden` | 403 | The key's access, or its maker's roles, do not allow this on something it can see |
| `api_key_scope` | 403 | The route is outside the key's areas |
| `cross_site` | 403 | A browser request without the CSRF header (sessions only) |
| `not_found` | 404 | It does not exist, or is outside the key's reach |
| `conflict` | 409 | The current state does not allow it, like a silence already over; `error` says why |
| `idempotency_in_progress` | 409 | The first request with this `Idempotency-Key` is still running |
| `gone` | 410 | A one-time link that was used or expired (not in v1) |
| `idempotency_key_reused` | 422 | This `Idempotency-Key` was used for another request |
| `rate_limited` | 429 | Over the key's rate limit |
| `internal` | 500 | Something failed on the central server; the details are in its log |
| `metrics_unavailable` | 502 | The metrics database is unreachable, failing or not configured |
| `logs_unavailable` | 502 | The logs database is unreachable, failing or not configured |
| `metrics_timeout` | 504 | The metrics database did not answer in time |
| `logs_timeout` | 504 | The logs database did not answer in time |

## Idempotency keys

A `POST`, `PUT` or `DELETE` made with a key may carry `Idempotency-Key`: 1 to 255 visible ASCII characters, a UUID usually. The first request with a value runs and its answer is kept for 24 hours. The same request again (same method, path, query and body) gets that answer back with `Idempotent-Replayed: true`, instead of running a second time. A script that lost its connection can then retry without opening two silences or queuing two updates.

- The same value with another request answers 422 `idempotency_key_reused`.
- While the first request is still running, a retry answers 409 `idempotency_in_progress`; try again a moment later.
- Answers of 500 and above are not kept, so a retry runs again. Answers over 1 MiB are not kept either.
- Answers that hand out a secret once (tokens, install keys, signing secrets) are not stored: a replay says it was done, without the secret.
- Values belong to a key: two keys never see each other's answers.

Without the header, writes behave as usual. Most are safe to repeat anyway, like acknowledging an incident or setting a value; the operations that are not say so.

## Rate limits

Each key may make 600 requests a minute, counted in fixed one-minute windows on each central server. Every answer to a key carries:

- `RateLimit-Limit`: requests allowed in a window, 600.
- `RateLimit-Remaining`: requests left in the current window.
- `RateLimit-Reset`: seconds until the window ends.

Over the limit, requests answer 429 `rate_limited` with `Retry-After`, in seconds. Requests made in a browser session are not limited.

For servers without Internet access: imports a release from its files,
sent as `multipart/form-data` up to 2 GiB in all. The signature of
`SHA256SUMS` is checked against the release keys built into the server
and every file against its checksum, as `agent-release import` does on
the command line. The release is then served to install commands and
agent and relay updates. Audited as `agent_release.import`.

Global administrators only: the release cache serves every customer.
Through an API key: access "Administer", reach everything, the
"updates" area. One import at a time. `Idempotency-Key` is ignored on
this route: importing the same release again replaces it with the same
files.

One page of the incidents of the servers and relays within the key's reach: open ones first, then the newest first. An incident is opened when a threshold is crossed (`metric` is then the metric) or when a server or relay stops reporting (`metric` is `offline`).

**Who**: any role. **Area**: `alerts`.

**Filters**, all optional and ANDed: `state`, `severity` (the current one), `server_id`, `site_id`, `from` and `to` (incidents active at some point between them), and `group` (the incidents one notification sent together, from the link in that notification). **Pages**: `limit` incidents per page, 1 to 500, 100 by default; pass `next_cursor` as `cursor` with the same filters for the next page, `null` on the last one.

A PSA polling for new alerts can ask for `state=open` every minute, and acknowledge what it took.

post.description:
Makes a reusable key for the install commands of a site. An `agent` key
enrolls up to `max_hosts` servers (no limit by default) until it expires
(30 days by default), each named after its host name; with
`require_approval`, each new host waits in `pending_hosts` until an
administrator approves it. A `relay` key enrolls one relay within a day
by default; `max_hosts` and `require_approval` are ignored for it, and
the relay waits for an administrator to confirm its names.

The answer is the only time the secret `token` is shown: MonitorFlow

object of a new token.

4096 bytes. Absent, or the same as the proposal, runs the proposal.

setting.

The rule that decided: `{"source": "builtin", "id": "readonly.df"}`

logged.

`posix` (the default) for Linux servers, `powershell` for Windows

customer-wide rules only.

default.

page lets administrators change.

in this answer only; MonitorFlow keeps only its hash.

Whether the nearest administrators of the incident's place are
told: of its site, else its customer, else everything.

Minutes without acknowledgement before telling, counted from the

The nearest administrators of the incident's place who can be told:
of its site, else its customer, else everything.

Minutes without acknowledgement before telling, 1 to 1440,
counted from the step before or from the first message.

on_call.description: Schedules whose person on call is told, or who covers their gap.

`waiting` for the next step at `next_at`, `silenced` until a silence
ends then waiting, or `stopped`.

When stopped: `acknowledged`, `resolved`, `not_critical`, or
`finished` once every step was told.

How many incidents it told that the user may read, this one

follow-up started: a warning, or not sent yet.

One incident. Field names and types are part of the API contract: add
fields, never rename or remove them.

Who said they are on it, and when (ADR-0082); `null` until someone
does. The name stays when the account is removed.

What they said they are doing (ADR-0130); `null` from a
notification link, or from an API key that sent none.

Whether the reader may acknowledge it: open, not acknowledged, and
the reader an operator or above of its site.

administrator confirms (ADR-0066), so it takes no host limit or

Validity in seconds, 3600 (one hour) to 31536000 (one year);

`revoked` first, then `expired`, then `used_up` once `host_count`

tags.name: remediation
tags.description: What the AI did about alerts. Each remediation incident is one alert the AI worked on, with every step recorded in a hash chain: the context it was sent after redaction, its proposals, how the rules classified each command, who approved or rejected it, and what the agent ran and printed. Read-only, except the approval queue, where people decide the commands the rules parked for them. The AI's text is untrusted: show it as data. Needs the key area "remediation".

tags.name: sensors
tags.description: What each server checks and how often. A server runs the built-in checks (cpu, memory, disk and disk activity, every minute or at its site's interval), overlaid with its site's rows, then its own: a row replaces the sensor of the same name and instance below it, and a disabled row removes it. Agents pick up a change within seconds; the effective view says whether the agent runs the current configuration. Offline alerts and the site's check interval are here too. Area `alerts`.

tags.name: thresholds
tags.description: When a metric opens an incident. Every server is checked against the built-in thresholds (CPU, memory, disk space, disk wait), overlaid with its site's rows, then its own: a row replaces the threshold of the same metric and instance below it, and a disabled row turns it off. A threshold opens a warning or critical incident once the value has stayed past it for `duration_s`, and resolves it once the value is back by more than the recovery margin (`hysteresis`). Area `alerts`.

tags.name: notifications
tags.description: Notification channels: where messages to people go when an incident opens, gets worse or ends, a command waits for approval, an update fails, a backup fails or a new version is out. A channel is an email address list sent through a mail server, a webhook, a chat channel (`slack`, `teams`, `discord`) or a plugin's, and notifies about everything, one customer or one site. Only administrators reach channels, and only those of what they administer: everything takes a global administrator (a key with every reach), a customer an administrator of it, a site an administrator of it or of its customer; others answer 404. Secrets are write-only: the mail password, signing secret, chat webhook URL or plugin secret settings go in `secret` and never come back, a channel says only `has_secret`, and a webhook shows only its URL's origin, as its path and query often hold a token. A channel saved by anyone but a global administrator only sends to public addresses. Every change is in the audit log, with the key's ID. API keys need the `alerts` area. For machines rather than people, use an integration.

tags.name: integrations
tags.description: Integrations: another tool, like a PSA or an automation, that gets MonitorFlow's events as one signed JSON `POST` per event: incidents, servers, updates, campaigns and approvals, each integration choosing which. The body follows [`docs/events/v1.schema.json`](https://github.com/Kidoly/monitorflow/blob/main/docs/events/v1.schema.json); the receiver's rules and code to check signatures are in [`docs/integrations.md`](https://github.com/Kidoly/monitorflow/blob/main/docs/integrations.md). In short: each request carries `X-MonitorFlow-Event`, `X-MonitorFlow-Delivery` (the event's `id`), `X-MonitorFlow-Timestamp` and `X-MonitorFlow-Signature`, `sha256=` and the HMAC-SHA256 of `{timestamp}.{raw body}` under the integration's signing secret, plus `X-MonitorFlow-Replay: 1` when sent again. Delivery is at least once: de-duplicate on the `id`. Anything but a 2xx within 15 seconds is retried after 30 seconds, then twice as long each time up to an hour, for 24 hours; an integration that accepts nothing for 24 hours is turned off and administrators are told. Events are kept 30 days and can be sent again with the same IDs. An integration notifies about everything, one customer or one site, and is managed by the administrators of that place, like a notification channel; others get 404. The URL and the signing secret are write-only: answers show the URL's origin, as its path and query often hold a token, and the secret only once, when it is made. Private and local addresses need a global administrator (a key with every reach). Every change is in the audit log, with the key's ID. API keys need the `administration` area.

tags.name: on-call
tags.description: On call: who is told of each alert of a place in person, besides the channels, in turns. A schedule is for everything, one customer or one site; its members take turns, handing off every day or every week at a local time in its time zone, and a cover puts someone else on call for a period. A gap is a period when the person on call cannot be told (no contact, disabled, removed, no longer sees the place); the nearest administrators are told instead. Schedules are managed by the administrators of their place, like notification channels: everything takes a global administrator (a key with every reach), a customer an administrator of it, a site an administrator of it or of its customer; others get 404. Only people who see all of the place can be put on a schedule. How each person is reached is theirs to set and not in the public API. Every change is in the audit log, with the key's ID. API keys need the `alerts` area.

tags.name: follow-up
tags.description: Follow-up: who is told next when nobody acknowledges a critical incident, step after step, for everything, one customer or one site. A step waits a number of minutes without acknowledgement, then tells the person on call of schedules, named people, notification channels or the nearest administrators. Where no follow-up is set, the default applies: the nearest administrators, after 15 minutes, once. The most precise follow-up of an incident's place applies: its site's, else its customer's, else everything's. An incident shows where it is in its follow-up (`GET /api/v1/incidents/{id}`), and acknowledging it stops the follow-up. Follow-ups are managed by the administrators of their place, like notification channels; others get 404, or 403 when saving. Every change is in the audit log, with the key's ID. API keys need the `alerts` area.

tags.name: enrollment
tags.description: Bringing servers and relays into MonitorFlow. An enrollment token is single-use: it enrolls one named server or relay on one site within its validity (one hour by default). An install key is reusable: it enrolls any number of servers (or one relay) on one site for up to a year, names each after its host, and can make new hosts wait for an administrator's approval. Both are secrets shown once, in the answer that creates them; no route returns them again and an `Idempotency-Key` replay does not either. Every route needs the administrator role on the site's customer, given globally or for that customer: a site's administrator cannot enroll. Through an API key, that means access "Administer", the "administration" area, and a reach of everything or of the customer.

tags.name: relays
tags.description: Relays: one per site where servers cannot reach the central server, or should not each open a connection to it. A relay forwards its site's agents to the central server, can serve package mirrors and releases on its network, and is enrolled like a server. Reading relays needs any role on their site; removing, updating and confirming the names of one needs the administrator role on its customer. Through an API key, relays are in the "servers" area, their updates in "updates"; listing them is open to any key within its reach.

tags.name: agent releases
tags.description: The MonitorFlow releases this server holds and serves to install commands and to agent and relay updates, so that servers without Internet access can install and update. Every release is checked against the release keys built into the server before it is kept. Importing one is for global administrators, since every customer uses the same releases.

tags.name: mirrors
tags.description: Package mirrors: copies of the apt and dnf repositories of the distributions servers run, kept on this server and on relays, so servers update without reaching the Internet and every server of a campaign installs the same packages. A mirror syncs on a schedule; a snapshot freezes what a sync copied under a name and never changes, and `current` is the newest one. Mirrors are shared by every customer, so every route is for global administrators: through an API key, access "Administer", reach everything and the "updates" area.

tags.name: package sources
tags.description: Where a server's apt or dnf takes its packages from: its own sources or the mirrors of this install. Changing them sends the server a signed `configure_sources` or `revert_sources` command, which the agent applies and can undo. Reading them needs any role on the server's site; changing them needs the administrator role on its customer. Through an API key, these routes are in the "updates" area. Windows servers have no mirror: their status says where Windows Update takes their updates from instead.

tags.name: risk rules
tags.description: How MonitorFlow decides what an AI command may do. Every command the AI proposes is classified by rules, never by the AI: `read_only` runs at once, `low_impact` waits for a person with an approver role unless the site's policy lets it run on its own, `high_impact` waits for an administrator, and `forbidden` never runs and hands the incident to a person. Built-in rules cover the commands MonitorFlow knows; administrators add allow rules for other commands (read-only or low impact only), deny patterns that forbid commands, and cache directories that may be cleared, for a customer or one of its sites. Rules and policies need a role on the customer as a whole (everything, or the customer): a role on one site, or a key that reaches one site, sees none. They need the key area "remediation".
